title: Hierarchical Retrieval at Scale: Bridging Interpretability and Efficiency
claim: A learned tree routes encoded query and context embeddings to leaf and intermediate assignments, and its nodes form coherent, human-readable semantic groups.
layout: 2 panels side by side; (a) top-down architecture, (b) annotated tree with callouts
description: Panel (a) shows the architecture. A Bi-Encoder box at the top encodes an example query ("Who is the voice of tony the tiger?") and a context passage into colored embedding strips. Dashed arrows carry these into a Tree Organizer, which is a binary tree of blue split nodes A–G. Routing probabilities such as 0.51 and 0.49 are written beside the nodes. The leaf level is a row of blue bars. Below it, purple query-assignment cells and orange context-assignment cells hold probability values, linked by a double-headed arrow labeled contrastive loss. A legend marks split and leaf nodes. Panel (b) shows a green and blue tree learned on NQ, with nodes 0, 2, 5, 11, 12 and 26. Pink and yellow speech-bubble callouts name topics (Media, Publishing, TV, Manga Comics) and list keywords. The eye goes first to the colorful tree in (a), then to the callouts.
caption: (a) During training, a positive query–context pair is encoded by the frozen Bi-Encoder E; these embeddings pass through each split node of a depth-D tree to yield left/right routing probabilities, which are merged into a leaf-assignment vector (one probability per leaf). At inference, leaf-level probabilities provide fine representations and intermediate-node probabilities serve as coarser representations. (b) Visualization of the topics (bold) and keywords extracted from the contexts assigned to one subtree (in green) rooted at node 5 of a ReTreever tree of depth 10 trained on NQ. For compactness, we represent only a subset of the nodes,and stop at depth 5. Topics are locally coherent along a path, indicating that ReTreever naturally groups contexts semantically.
abstract: Information retrieval is a core component of many intelligent systems as it enables conditioning of outputs on new and large-scale datasets. While effective, the standard practice of encoding data into high-dimensional representations for similarity search entails large memory and compute footprints, and also makes it hard to inspect the inner workings of the system. Hierarchical retrieval methods offer an interpretable alternative by organizing data at multiple granular levels, yet do not match the efficiency and performance of flat retrieval approaches. In this paper, we propose Retreever, a tree-based method that makes hierarchical retrieval viable at scale by directly optimizing its structure for retrieval performance while naturally providing transparency through meaningful semantic groupings. Our method offers the flexibility to balance cost and utility by indexing data using representations from any tree level. We show that Retreever delivers strong coarse (intermediate levels) and fine representations (terminal level), while achieving the highest retrieval accuracy at the lowest latency among hierarchical methods. These results demonstrate that this family of techniques is viable in practical applications.
